title: Chapter 55: The Vault Under the Dome, Part 2 of 5: Door Three
html:
At twenty to midnight he put the tray down on the little gilt table by the wall, with the decanter and the two glasses on it, and walked away from it.
That was the hardest part. Harder than the lamp at the kitchen gate. Harder than Gorse. Just to put the tray down and turn his back on it and walk to the servants' door behind the gallery stair, at Fenton's pace, with his stiff leg swinging, while five hundred people stood in the hall behind him with their backs to him. Without looking round. Without looking at the gray gown by the table of loves. Without looking at the plain chair by the brass box.
He did it.
The servants' door was low, with plum velvet over it on the hall side and plain boards on the other. He pushed through it. And the heat and the light and the music were behind him, muffled, like sounds through a wall, and he was in a passage.
It was narrow and bare and dim, lit by one lamp on a hook, with a floor of worn stone and walls of whitewash gone gray with the hands of a thousand servants. It went left and right. Left was the stair down to the servants' hall. Right was the way to the kitchens, and the kitchen yard.
He went right.
The passage turned. And turned again. Past the open door of a pantry, where a boy in plum was asleep on a sack with his mouth open. Past a scullery, steaming, full of women up to their elbows in gray water, singing. Past a door with a brass plate on it that said HOUSEKEEPER, shut. Past a room full of ice, blocks of it, stacked like bricks, with a man in a leather apron chipping at one with a pick, who did not look up.
And then a door with a bar across it. And on the other side of the door, the cold.
The kitchen yard. But not the part with the carts. The back of it. Behind the gallery. A narrow space between the high black wall of the Bourse on one side and the high stone wall of the yard on the other, open to the sky. The snow was coming down into it, out of the dark, through the light of one small lamp on the Bourse wall. It was very quiet here. He could hear the music from the hall, faint, through the stone. And the river, somewhere beyond the yard wall, slapping. And his own breath.
And there were doors.
A row of them, in the black wall of the Bourse. Narrow doors, each one iron-studded and painted black, each one with a number painted over it in white. Old numbers. Faded. 1. 2. 3. All the way along. Twelve of them. The upstairs doors, Gideon had said. V keys. Upstairs. One to twelve.
At the doors from one to twelve, Wren's list had said, one watcher each, in the Lady's livery. Except door three.
He could see them. Down the row. A man in plum standing in front of each black door, with his back to it and his hands behind him, in the snow. Very still. Like the white guards at the palace gate. Eleven of them. One at door one. One at door two. One at door four. One at five.
At door three there were two men.
Not in plum.
In gray. A soft pale gray, like a dove's back, with silver buttons, and silver at the cuffs. Long gray coats, and gray gloves, and plain gray hats. They stood on either side of door three, not in front of it, and they were not looking at the yard. They were looking at him.
The Bank's livery. The Treasurer's.
NOT door 3: no post, the Treasurer's (D.S.) own men.
Corin walked toward them. At Fenton's pace. With the snow coming down on Fenton's gray hair and Fenton's gold coat, and his stiff leg swinging, and his stick ringing on the frozen cobbles. Past door one, and its watcher in plum, who did not turn his head. Past door two.
He stopped in front of door three.
The two men in gray looked at him.
They were young. About Remy's age. Clean-shaven, with smooth pleasant faces, very alike, like brothers, or like two men who had been chosen because they looked like nothing at all. They looked at his gold coat. At his sour face. At his stick. At his scorched white gloves.
And the one on the left said, quite pleasantly, in a low voice:
"You're late, Mr. Fenton."
Corin did not move.
"The Treasurer said a quarter to," said the young man. He took a watch out of his own gray waistcoat. A small silver one. He looked at it. "It's twelve minutes to." He put the watch away. "He said you might be. He said you'd have trouble at the kitchen gate. With the lamp." He looked down at Corin's gloves. At the brown at the fingertips. "He said to tell you he was sorry about the lamp. It wasn't his to put out."
The snow came down between them.
Corin said nothing. He did not know what to say. He did not know if Fenton would say anything. He did not know who he was supposed to be, in front of these two young men in gray, who knew exactly who he was.
The one on the right stepped forward.
"You'll have a key," he said. Not a question.
Corin put his hand inside the gold coat. Into the inside pocket, over his heart, where the Ledger was. And took the Ledger out. And opened it, at the back, where the key was. A brass key, with a worn bow, and new teeth, stamped V and 3. He had kept it there since Wednesday, since Lyra took it out of the little gray pocket in the mask and gave it to him in the crypt.
He held it out.
The young man in gray did not take it. He looked at it. At the new teeth.
"That's right," he said. "That's the one. The lock was changed on Monday morning, the way it always is, the week before. The Treasurer's locksmith did it." He paused. "The Treasurer always uses his own locksmith. For door three."
Or somebody is the locksmith, Oren had said. On Wednesday. In the crypt.
"Go on, then," said the young man on the left. Pleasantly. "Up the stair goes to the Fourth Tier rooms. The waiters will be coming through in a minute or two, for the quarter. You don't want to be on the stair when they come." He paused. "Down the stair goes where you're going. There's a young man waiting on it, below the gallery. He's been waiting a while."
Corin looked at him.
"Why?" he said.
It came out in his own voice. Not Fenton's. He heard it. So did they.
The young man on the left did not seem surprised.
"The Treasurer said you'd ask that," he said. "He said to tell you: Because a man who wants a thing badly enough to walk into this house on one leg is a man worth owing a favor to." He tilted his head a little. "And he said to tell you one more thing. He said: Mind the ninth step."
The snow came down.
The ninth step. The kitchen stair. On Tuesday night. Where Corin had sat with his leg stuck out across the step and could not get up, and the Auditor had come down past him with a lamp boy holding a lamp in front of her, and afterward had knelt and touched the blood he left there with her bare fingers.
The Treasurer knew about the ninth step.
The Treasurer knew everything.
Corin put the brass key into the lock of door three.
It went in smoothly. It turned without a sound. Somebody had oiled this lock too. He felt the bolt go back inside the door. And the door moved, a little, inward, under his hand.
"Mr. Fenton," said the young man on the right.
Corin looked at him.
"Midnight," said the young man. "When the box is opened. When the Lady reads out the names. Whatever happens then." He looked up, past Corin, at the black wall of the Bourse going up into the dark and the snow. At the glow of the dome over it. "Don't come back this way."
Then he stepped back to his place beside door three, and folded his gray-gloved hands behind his back, and looked at the yard. And so did the other one. As if Corin were not there. As if he had never been there.
Corin pushed the door open.
And went through it, into the dark. And pulled it shut behind him. And stood for a moment with his back against it, on a stone landing, at the bottom of a stair that went up into the dark on his left and down into the dark on his right, and breathed.
Above him, very faint, he heard footsteps. Many of them. Coming down from somewhere high up. The waiters. Coming for the quarter.
Below him, nothing. Just the dark. And the cold. And very faintly, a smell. Wet stone. Ice. And something else. Something like the inside of a jar that has been sealed for a very long time.
And a voice.
Quite close. A few steps below him, in the dark. Low and quick and careful.
"You're late," said Remy Castellan.
The Back Stair
Remy was sitting on the seventh step down, in the dark, with his knees drawn up and his bare hands hanging between them, the way Silas had sat on the step of Saint Bride's.
Corin could see him only as a shape. A thin pale shape in a gray coat, against the black of the stair, lit very faintly from below by something Corin could not see. A gray glow. Coming up the stair from far down, from round the turn, cold and steady, like moonlight under a door.
Remy got up.
He did it quickly, all at once, the way young men get up. And came up the six steps to the landing, and stopped one step below Corin, and looked at him. At the long sour face. At the gray beard. At the gold livery.
"Vespera," said Remy.
"Yes."
"It's very good." He looked a moment longer. "I'd never have known you. I passed you twice in the hall tonight, with the Lady's fan, and I never knew you." A pause. "I knew your hands, though. When you put the tray down. The way you put it down. Both hands, as if it could feel it."
You used to put the jars back on the shelf with both hands, Linus Hale had said. As if they could feel it.
Corin did not say anything.
Above them, on the stair going up, the footsteps were nearer. Many feet. Coming down. And voices now, low, men's voices, and the clink of glass on silver. The waiters. Coming down from the Fourth Tier rooms for the quarter.
"Down," said Remy. "Now."
They went down.
Corin had thought, on the Garden Steps on Saturday, that going down was worse than going up. He had been right. This stair was worse than the Garden Steps. It was narrow, and it turned, and turned, round and round a stone pillar in the middle like the stair in the tower at Saint Bride's, and the steps were worn hollow in the middle and wet, and there was no rail. Only the wall, on the outside, rough and cold and wet under his hand. He went down the way Silas had taught him. Sideways. The stick first. Then the bad leg, swung out stiff and lowered onto the step below, heel first. Then the good one after it. Down with the bad.
Remy went in front of him. Backward. One step below him all the way, facing up, the way Juno had on the Garden Steps. With his bare hands held out a little, ready. He was stronger than Juno. If Corin fell, Remy would catch him. They both knew it.
Above them, the waiters reached the landing. Corin heard them pass. Heard the door to the kitchen yard open, and the cold come in, and the clink of glass, and the door close. And then they were gone, and there was only the stair, and the dark, and the gray glow coming up from below.
"How long have you been waiting?" said Corin.
"Since the eleventh bell." Remy's voice was low and even. "I left the Lady's box when she rang for the bidding. She didn't notice. She doesn't notice me when she's afraid." He went down another step, backward. "She's afraid tonight. More than I've ever seen her."
"Because of him."
Remy did not ask who. He did not need to.
"She was told at the eighth bell," he said. "A boy came from the Hill with a card. She read it, and then she sat very still in her chair in her dressing room for a long time with the card in her lap, and then she called Hollis and told him to have the garden door opened and the hinges oiled." A pause. "And then she called me, and told me to wear my gray coat, and not the plum, and to stand behind her chair all night and not leave it for anything."
"And you left it."
"Yes," said Remy. "I left it."
They went down. Round and round. The gray glow got brighter. And the cold.
"There's something else," said Remy.
Corin waited.
"The Inquisitor's men," said Remy. "The list said a few. Six on the front steps, four on Exchange Street, two in Cinder Lane, two in the kitchen yard, four in a boat at the wet door, two on the roof. Twenty. And the Inquisitor himself, and his cadet, in the gallery." He went down another step. "I counted them, at the eleventh bell, from the Lady's box, through the glass of the dome. On the roofs of Exchange Street. In the doorways. In the boats on the river." He was quiet a moment. "There are more than twenty, Vane. Many more. Forty, at least. Maybe sixty. In gray coats, and black ones. Waiting. Not watching the Bourse. Watching the doors of the Bourse. All of them." Another step. "The way you watch the doors of a house you mean to go into."
Corin stopped on the stair.
"He's not here for the box," said Remy quietly. "I don't think he's here for the box at all. I don't know what he's here for. But it isn't the box."
They looked at each other in the gray light. A young man with ink on his cuff and scars on his thumbs, and a sour old cellarman with another man's face and scorched white gloves.
"Then we're quick," said Corin.
"Yes," said Remy. "We're quick."
The stair ended.
It ended at a door. Not wood. Iron. A great flat round-topped slab of black iron, set into the stone at the bottom of the stair, with no handle and no lock and no hinge that Corin could see. The gray glow was coming from round its edges. A thin line of light, all the way round, where the iron met the stone, like the light round a lid on a pot.
And it hummed.
Corin felt it before he heard it. In his teeth. In his gray hands, under the scorched gloves. A deep low steady hum, below hearing almost, like the note of a great bell that has been struck a long time ago and is still, very faintly, ringing. He had felt it before. On Sunday night, a week ago, in the ring passage under the Bourse, crouching in the dark with Gideon. A barred iron humming door on the north side. It remembers you.
This was the same door. From the other side.
Remy took a little knife out of his coat pocket.
It was very small. A penknife, with a handle of white bone and a blade no longer than his little finger. He opened it. He looked at his left thumb, in the gray light. At the pad of it, which was crossed all over with fine white scars, like the lines on an old map. Dozens of them. Corin had seen them on Tuesday, in the arches. He had not counted them then. He did not count them now.
Remy cut his thumb.
He did it quickly, without looking, the way a man does a thing he has done a thousand times. A short shallow cut, across the pad, beside the last scar. Blood came up at once, dark and bright. He closed the knife and put it away. And put his bleeding thumb flat against the black iron of the door, in the middle, at the height of his heart.
The hum changed.
It went up. Not louder. Higher. A note going up, the way a voice goes up when it is asking a question. Corin felt it in his teeth. And then it stopped. All at once. Silence. So sudden and so complete that his ears rang with it.
And the door opened.
Not on hinges. It slid. Sideways, into the stone, slowly, with a long low grinding sigh, like a great breath being let out. And the gray light came out round it, and then through it, and Corin had to put his scorched gloved hand up over Fenton's eyes.
When he took it away, the door was gone into the wall. And beyond it, going away into the dark, there was glass.
Remy took his thumb off the iron. There was a small dark smear where it had been. He looked at it for a moment. Then he wiped his thumb on the inside of his gray coat, very carefully, the way he did everything, and turned to Corin.
"She opened this door for me the first time when I was six," he said. "She held my hand and cut my thumb herself and put it on the iron. And she said, There. Now it knows you. Now you're mine." He looked at the dark smear on the door. "I've opened it four hundred and three times since. I counted. I keep it in my book." He paused. "This is the first time I've opened it for somebody she doesn't know about."
He held out his hand. His bare hand. The cut one.
"Hold on," said Remy Castellan. "And think of nothing. The glass knows you now. But it'll still look."
